title: Authorized-Aftermarket Legacy DRAM Die Bank (+ hi-rel MCMs)
status_reason: No objection was refuted. All three FATALs were confirmed by the model, and they kill L1, the managed die-bank program and the only line this founder could run. Banking bare die costs a board OEM $186k-347k to manage ~$52k of die, 2.9-5.4x a packaged last-time buy plus dry storage. Board OEMs qualify packaged part numbers, and Micross sells the whole bundle direct (EDSP). L3, the title-taking bank, is killed by the completed pull-cost stack (RT-VET-DD7-03) plus bare-die storage yield, surveillance, whole-wafer pulls and a 2.0x blended multiple. Bought at m20 in BASE it has unit GM -12.8% and IRR -26.6%, and no bank is bought in any scenario; break-even needs <=$1.53/die all-in. Plan C is killed on founder constraints. L4, the MCM, survives only as a capital-heavy option. It needs a stacked/RDL redesign, a 125 C bin and per-lot requalification, and Plan B now returns 0.29x on $11.49M (GLUT 0.24x, SEVERE 0.19x). The moat (OCM authorized-aftermarket rights) was never tested, and the evidence says the OCMs that would talk are extending their lines. What remains, L2 rep commissions ($8.6k BASE m36 ARR, never breaking even at Phase 4 fixed costs), is not this concept. It also costs DD6 time.

revised_verdicts.possible: Only for incumbents (revised after red team). Rochester, Micross and Teledyne prove the businesses at scale, but each leg fails for an entrant. 10-20-year bare-die DRAM storage is TRL 6-7: no published bondability or yield data past ~3 years, and Infineon caps unsawn wafers in N2 at 36 months. The 8 GB x72 MCM as described does not fit 15 x 20 mm (405-675 mm2 of die). It needs stacking with whole-wafer RDL, and JEDEC specifies no DDR4 refresh above 95 C, so a 125 C part needs a per-die hot bin and a refresh derate (23-72% refresh tax). An unauthorized re-packaged die is a new part number, so it cannot serve DO-254 or FDA locks.
revised_verdicts.profitable: No (revised after red team). L1 costs the OEM 2.9-5.4x a packaged LTB, so it has no rational buyer. The revised bank loses money in every scenario: BASE m20 unit GM -12.8% and IRR -26.6%; GLUT -109% and -99.4%. IRR break-even needs <=$1.53/die all-in pull cost. Plan B returns 0.29x of $11.49M outside capital in BASE (0.24x GLUT, 0.19x SEVERE). Year-10 EBITDA is -$1.10M; MCM GM is 18.7/26.7/38.2% (m1/m36/m60); the BULL case is ~22%/yr gross before dilution over 10 years. The residual L2 rep line reaches $5.0k ARR at m18 and $8.6k at m36 in BASE ($4.4k GLUT, $928 SEVERE) and never breaks even at $680/month of fixed cost.
revised_verdicts.doable: No (revised after red team). The founder-doable wedge (L1) has no rational buyer. DoD-facing study work needs NIST SP 800-171 compliance (~$35k + $500/month) and defense-OEM agency needs AS9120B (~$35k); each breaks the $20k cash floor by m6. The bank and the MCM need OCM authorization, a hi-rel co-founder and ~$11.5M. On DD6's Phase 4 inputs, every 10 hours a month diverted to DD7 moved DD6's full-time switch from m23 to m33, and 20 hours meant never; on DD6's revised (Phase 5) model DD6 is never full-time, and 10 / 20 hours a month cut its m36 ARR from $63.9k to $56.2k / $45.3k (model §10h). The residual rep line also needs an employer carve-out.

ev_note: After the red team the expected value of DD7 for this founder is about zero to slightly negative. No line clears unit economics at entrant scale, and the moat cannot be obtained. The only residual is L2 rep commissions, worth $8.6k of BASE m36 ARR if a rep offer arrives and ~$2.2k probability-weighted at p = 0.25. It never breaks even at Phase 4 fixed costs (cash below $20k at m22), and only a lean $300/month set-up breaks even, at m15. Every DD7 hour costs DD6: on DD6's Phase 4 inputs 10 h/month moved its full-time switch from m23 to m33; on DD6's revised model it cuts DD6's m36 ARR from $63.9k to $56.2k (model §10h). Role: DROP. It is not a MOONSHOT candidate: Plan B returns 0.29x on $11.49M, and BULL is ~22%/yr gross before dilution over 10 years with a design that must first be re-engineered. It is not a FALLBACK, because it never pays the founder in any scenario. It is not a side line, because it conflicts with DD6's hours and with the day-job employer. Do not run the 29-day kill test; that saves ~$6k and ~50 hours. Residue at $0: (a) one paragraph of packaged-part dry-storage advice inside DD2's LTB study; (b) a passive watch. Reopen C-91 only on a written OCM offer of authorized-aftermarket rights for a named EOL DRAM part. Reopen C-65 only if a hi-rel co-founder brings an existing x72 design-in plus >=3 evaluation LOIs at >=$1,200.

responses.response: Correct, and the model confirms it. One L1 program's die are worth $51.9k as KGD at the 2026 peak ($61.1k as packaged parts). Phase 4 was internally inconsistent: it charged L3 a $40-120k package-and-test set-up per part family but let L1 pull die through an OSAT at ~$10 with no set-up at all. Model §10b prices the OEM's whole die-bank route: die + founder billing + U.S. package/test ($10-12.11/die) + vault (3%/yr, or a $5k/yr minimum) + set-up. That is $186k-289k if the die are drawn at 80/month (exhausted in 50 months), and $230k-347k over the model's 100-month program life. Against ~$64k for a packaged LTB plus dry or N2 storage under GEIA-STD-0003B/IEC 62435, it is 2.9-5.4x. The die-supply point also stands. Micron sells no open KGD, so a board carrying Micron or Samsung DDR4 cannot bank its own die. A Winbond/ESMT die is a different die and forces the requalification the LTB was meant to avoid. The bare-die users (Teledyne, Mercury, Frontgrade, Micross, DDC) run their own vaults, and Micross sells the whole bundle (EDSP; RT-VC-DD7-02). On the re-spec route: packaged-part LTB storage management is DD2's LTB study plus a storage recommendation. A $750/month fee on $61k of packaged parts is ~14.7% a year of inventory value. I have no quote showing Micross, Rochester or distributors don't already offer storage, so the would-change-my-mind test is not met. L1 is killed. Without it Plan A is L2 rep commissions only: revised BASE m36 recurring ARR is $8,606 ($4,389 GLUT, $928 SEVERE), versus Phase 4's $42.6k. It never breaks even at $680/month of fixed cost, and cash falls below the $20k floor at m22.
responses.action: Named leg L1 (managed die-bank programs) killed. Model: l1_enabled 1 -> 0 (RED-TEAM REVISIONS block); new l1_buyer_cost() and model §10b compare the OEM's die-bank cost with a packaged LTB. Plan A is now L2 only. Packaged-part LTB storage advice moves into DD2's LTB study as a free paragraph, not a DD7 SKU. Deep dive §0, §2, §10, §11 and §14 revised.

responses.response: Valid. An LTB study done for a NAVSUP, Tobyhanna or NAWC DMSMS awardee means receiving weapon-system BOMs and part-level obsolescence data. These are normally marked CUI (CTI or export-controlled), so DFARS 252.204-7012 flows down to the founder's LLC: the NIST SP 800-171 controls, an SPRS score under 252.204-7019/-7020, a compliant mail and file tenant, and 72-hour incident reporting. I could not verify the reported 2026-07-13 suspension of the CMMC Phase-2 C3PAO requirement (no search budget left), but the 800-171 obligation does not depend on it. Model §10c, on Phase 4 inputs: adding the reviewer's $35k one-off at m6 plus $500/month takes the Plan A cash low from $30.2k (m3) to -$3.7k (m6), through the $20k kill floor (§11 #8) at m6. Adding AS9120B as well (RT-HYP-DD7-03) takes it to -$40.5k. So the DoD DMSMS customers #1-3 were never reachable by a $40k part-time wedge. SAM/CAGE registration and DD Form 2345 were also missing from the plan.
responses.action: Customers #1-3 (DoD DMSMS work through primes) removed from every founder-funded plan. Model: variant hooks planA_extra_oneoff / planA_extra_month added, and the CUI case runs in §10c. Any reopening of DoD-facing study work needs either a prime's written statement that the inputs are not CUI/CTI, or ~$35k one-off + ~$500/month in the plan with cash still above $20k. SAM/CAGE and DD 2345 are listed as prerequisites in §11.

responses.response: Valid. In Plan A the founder sizes the buy, arranges the purchase, places the die in a vault and draws pulls. That puts them in the component chain of custody, so defense OEMs flow down DFARS 252.246-7007/-7008 and AS5553/AS6174-type terms and would approve them only with AS9120B (plus AS6081 or AS6496). Phase 4 put AS9120B in Plan B only. Model §10c, on Phase 4 inputs: AS9120B in year 1 ($35k over m2-m6, then $8k/yr from m14) breaks the $20k cash floor at m3 and takes cash to -$3.2k at m6. I have no written statement from #6-#8 that they would contract an uncertified program manager because custody sits with Micross and the OSAT. With L1 already killed on buyer economics, this closes the last route to defense OEMs for any agent-type service in a founder-funded plan.
responses.action: Defense OEMs #6-#7 dropped from founder-funded plans. AS9120B (and AS6081/AS6496) is recorded as a precondition for any procurement-agent role. Model §10c shows the year-1 AS9120B variant and the combined CUI + AS9120B variant (cash low -$40.5k).

responses.response: Valid. The bank sells from m38 (sell_lag 18 months after an m20 purchase), which is exactly when the 2019-22 Cascade Lake, Ice Lake and Milan fleets retire through ITAD (2028-30). Recovered packaged DDR4 caps the price for every buyer DFARS does not bind: rugged, industrial SBC, medical and rail (#6-#10). The 2.5x authorized multiple therefore applies mainly to the DoD slice, and that slice needs an OCM letter. Model §10d, on Phase 4 inputs (bank bought m20, BASE): at 1.5x, unit GM is -0.7% and IRR -15.3% (no buy). At a 2.0x blend, GM is 24.5%, which still passes the >=20% rule, but IRR is -5.0% and the cash multiple 0.77x. So the BASE bank's 2.6% IRR depended wholly on 2.5x across all sales.
responses.action: aftermarket_mult 2.5 -> 2.0 [ESTIMATE: 50/50 blend of 2.5x DFARS-bound and ~1.5x non-DFARS buyers]. The BASE m20 bank is no longer bought (revised model §5 and §10d). §12 cycle text notes ITAD supply in the sell window.

responses.response: Valid. A rep agreement makes the founder a sales agent, and a KGD quote makes them a customer. Neither is authorized-aftermarket status, where the OCM transfers wafers, test programs and marking rights for a named EOL part (ERAI definition, §1). Intelligent Memory and Alliance appoint reps and distributors routinely (IM added Sourceability and Flip in 2026), and ESMT KGD is already listed at Suntsu. So Track A and the m15 'OCM letter' gate could both pass while C-91's moat is false. With DD7 killed, the 29-day test is not run, but the rewritten Track A becomes the reopen condition. It requires a written OCM statement of willingness to grant aftermarket or continuity rights (die plus test-program transfer, and permission to mark) on at least one named EOL DDR3/DDR4 part to a new U.S. entity, with indicative terms. A rep or distribution offer scores only as L2. The rewritten bar is far less likely to be met, because the six named OCMs are extending their legacy lines rather than exiting (§5). That lowers the moat's probability, not just the test's rigor.
responses.action: Track A pass bar and the m15 Stage-1 gate rewritten as reopen conditions (§10, §11). A rep or distribution offer counts only toward L2. C-91's moat score of 4 is recorded as unsupported for an entrant (§14).

responses.response: Valid. The founder's day job is product development and operations at a design/manufacturing company, the same OEM type as targets #6-#8. A rep commission on DRAM sold to OEMs (L2), or managing an OEM's LTB buys (L1), is a textbook conflict under a standard invention-assignment and conflict-of-interest agreement. That holds especially if the employer buys from the represented maker or competes with the prospects. DD2 (RT-VC-DD2-05) and DD6 already gate on this; DD7 did not.
responses.action: New Step 0b / K0: a ~$500 employment-agreement review and a written employer carve-out covering component representation and LTB services, before any rep or OEM conversation; kill on refusal (§10, §11). Model: oneoff_m1 8,500 -> 3,900 ($500 employer review + $900 rep-agreement review + $2,500 LLC/rep legal; the $6,000 kill test is withdrawn). Economic effect ~$500.

responses.response: Valid. The $6.3-25.4M a year rests on an unsourced '~10% of DSPO cases are memory' and an assumed $50-200k per buy. It also measures the value of life-of-need buys, which are mostly packaged parts from franchised distributors or Rochester stock, not die-bank demand. DSPO's own table shows simple substitution resolving 2.2x as many cases as life-of-need buys (2,809 vs 1,268). Model §10i restates it as the founder's fee pool. ~127 memory life-of-need cases a year x $9.0k of program ARR = $1.14M of new ARR a year at 100% national share, plus $0.25-1.01M a year of one-off 4% agency fees. A 3-5% share gives $34-57k of new ARR a year. Because die-bank programs are now killed, even that pool is not addressable by this concept.
responses.action: §3's 'sanity ceiling' is withdrawn as a C-91 anchor and restated as a fee-pool ceiling (model §10i). DSPO substitution share added to §14.

responses.response: The arithmetic is right: nine 45 mm2 die are 405 mm2 of silicon, more than a whole 20 x 20 mm package (400 mm2) and 135% of a 15 x 20 mm one. On the 60-90 mm2 die that the legacy OCMs actually make it is 180-270% (model §10f). Search confirms the benchmark: Teledyne's DDR4T04G72 is a 15 x 20 x 1.92 mm, 391-ball multi-chip package on Micron die, sold in 4 GB and 8 GB versions [REPORTED, search 2026-11-01]. An 8 GB x72 in that footprint therefore needs 16Gb die or stacking. I found no legacy OCM offering 16Gb x16 DDR4 KGD [UNVERIFIED]. Stacking center-pad DDR4 needs a wafer-level RDL or a face-down window per die plus thinning to ~100 um. RDL is a whole-wafer step, which rules out distributor KGD and needs whole wafers or pre-RDL'd die. Model §10e reproduces the reviewer's re-run exactly. Substrate $90 + assembly $160 cuts unit GM from 45.6/52.2/61.8% to 32.1/38.8/48.4% (m1/m36/m60), and to 27.3/34.5/44.7% at 85% module yield. §6's 'low risk' FTO reading is withdrawn: stacked-memory packaging (3D Plus, Teledyne, the Irvine Sensors lineage) has not been searched.
responses.action: mcm_substrate 60 -> 90 and mcm_assembly 80 -> 160 (stacked/RDL build) [ESTIMATE]. The §1 MCM description is corrected to a stacked or larger-footprint part needing wafer or pre-RDL die supply. §6 FTO #4 changed from 'low risk' to 'not cleared'. The L4 reopen condition requires the reviewer's OSAT floorplan and quote.

responses.response: Valid in substance. JEDEC DDR4 defines tREFI 7.8 us to 85 C and 3.9 us to 95 C Tcase, and nothing above that (SK hynix datasheets via search, 2026-11-01) [REPORTED]. Model §10e reproduces the refresh tax with tRFC1 = 350 ns. Extending 2x per 10 C past 95 C gives 18%, 36% and 72% of device time at 105, 115 and 125 C. An Arrhenius fit with Ea 0.5-0.6 eV gives 23-32% at 125 C. One partial pushback: automotive-grade DRAM vendors do ship parts rated above 95 C with derated refresh [UNVERIFIED-training], so 125 C is a bin-and-derate problem, not an impossibility. But that confirms the reviewer's main point: every die needs a hot-retention bin, which distributor KGD probed at commercial or industrial temperature has not had. Bin yield enters as a ninth power. On Phase 4 inputs, 98%/die gives 0.834 module yield (GM 40.6/47.9/58.3%); 95% gives 0.630 (21.4/31.0/44.8%); 90% gives 0.387 (GM -27.9/-12.2/+10.2%).
responses.action: mcm_yield 0.91 -> 0.76, carrying a 3%/die fallout from the 125 C bin and screen together with RT-VET-DD7-04. The MCM's lead grade becomes -40 to 105 C, with 125 C as a binned option whose datasheet must state the refresh interval and bandwidth derate. The L4 reopen condition requires hot-retention bin data on >=100 die.

responses.response: Valid. pull_yield 0.95 cited Rochester's packaged-part study, where mold compound covers the pads. A banked wafer has exposed aluminium pads already carrying probe scrub from sort. Infineon's own limit for unsawn wafers in N2 is 36 months, and IEC 62435 has a whole part on deterioration mechanisms and says compliant storage does not guarantee working parts. I found no published bond-pull or yield data on DRAM die after >=10 years in nitrogen. Model §10d reproduces the reviewer's re-runs on Phase 4 inputs exactly: pull yield 0.90 gives GM 36.2% and IRR 0.8%; 0.85 gives 32.5%, -1.1% and 0.95x; 0.80 gives 28.3% and -3.2%. All of them pass the >=20% unit-GM rule, so that rule could not catch a storage miss. A $5k/yr surveillance programme (annual sample assembly, test, bond pull/shear) alone takes the Phase 4 IRR from 2.6% to -0.2%. 'TRL 9' holds for Rochester's packaged practice and for multi-year wafer storage. For 10-20-year bare DRAM die it is TRL 6-7.
responses.action: pull_yield 0.95 -> 0.90; surveillance_yr 0 -> $5,000 per bank per year. POSSIBLE verdict revised: 10-20-year bare-die DRAM storage is TRL 6-7. Bank buy rule (§11 #11) rewritten to need unit GM >=20% and a 10-year IRR above the hurdle at pull yield 0.85. That rule change is moot in the model because no bank passes even the old rule.

responses.response: Valid on the process point. Thinning and sawing (and RDL for stacks) are whole-wafer steps, so opening a wafer releases ~1,251 die (Phase 4 basis) or ~736 (revised basis), which then sit for 8-16 months singulated on tape or in waffle packs. I adopted the reviewer's option (a): package the whole wafer when it is opened and store packaged parts, the mode Rochester's 17-year data supports. The model now books each wafer's full pull cost when it is opened. The money effect is small: on Phase 4 inputs the BASE IRR moves from 2.64% to 2.57%, and the cash multiple stays 1.13x. Whether QP Technologies or Integra can backgrind and saw 300 mm DRAM wafers is still unverified, and it is now a reopen condition.
responses.action: pull_whole_wafer False -> True; new pull_charge() books a wafer's pull cost at opening in both simulate() and bank_standalone(). A U.S. 300 mm backgrind/saw quote is added to the L3 reopen conditions.

responses.response: Valid on both counts. (1) The Suntsu lot named in §10 C4 is 'KGD 256Mbx16 DDR4', a 4Gb x16 die. An 8 GB x72 needs 18-20 of those, so buying it tests a die the design cannot use. (2) 1,251 good die per wafer assumes a 45 mm2 big-three die. Model §10f reproduces the reviewer's range for 60-90 mm2 legacy-OCM die: 928-608 good die per 300 mm wafer, so a 12,510-die bank is 13.5-20.6 wafers. As the reviewer predicted, bank economics do not move, because die are priced per GB: on Phase 4 inputs unit GM stays 39.6% and IRR 2.6%. The wafer counts and MCM silicon area do move, and they feed RT-PHY-DD7-01.
responses.action: good_die_per_wafer 1,251 -> 736 (75 mm2 midpoint) and bank_wafers 10 -> 17 (keeps ~12,500 die). The C4 KGD purchase is withdrawn with the kill test. Any reopened MCM work must name the exact 8Gb x8 die (size, node, die per wafer) in an OCM or distributor quote.

responses.response: Correct. Model §10b reproduces it. Over the 100-month life the founder bills $85.1k: $75k of fees, $2.1k of agency fee, the $4k study and $4k of pull margin. The die are worth $51.9k at the 2026 peak and ~$7.7k at the $3/GB long-run price (4,000 x 0.75 GB x 0.85 x $3). Adding the vault, U.S. package/test and the $40-120k set-up gives the OEM $230k-347k to manage ~$52k of die ($186k-289k if drawn in 50 months), against ~$64k for a packaged LTB plus storage. Checking this also found a Phase 4 bug the reviewer implied: program_unit billed $1 pulls at 80/month for 100 months, which is 8,000 pulls from a 4,000-die program. Lifetime gross profit per program falls from $79.1k to $75.1k once pulls are capped, before the p_program change. The FTO point holds too. Without OCM authorization a re-packaged die cannot carry the OCM part number, and the test program belongs to the OCM. A board OEM would therefore pull a different part number, which is the requalification the LTB was meant to avoid.
responses.action: Named leg L1 killed (l1_enabled 1 -> 0). pull_cap_to_ltb False -> True fixes the program_unit pull bug. Model §10b documents the buyer economics. Deep dive §0, §2, §10, §11 and §14 revised.

responses.response: Confirmed by search (2026-11-01, Micross pages and EDSP flyer via snippets) [REPORTED]. Micross's EOL Die Sustainment Program procures the LTB of die and wafers for OEMs and contract manufacturers. It holds them in nitrogen for 20+ years for an annual storage fee under a long-term agreement, offers consignment or pay-on-demand billing, keeps the authorized chain of custody, and ships drop-in die or fully packaged parts from the original qualified die. Program Sustainment Management adds BOM monitoring and supplier-managed inventory. That is the whole L1 bundle, sold by an IBAS-funded incumbent with a $134.3M ceiling. A part-time $750/month layer adds nothing an OEM cannot buy direct. Model §10c, on Phase 4 inputs: p_program 0.35 -> 0.10 cuts Plan A m36 ARR from $42.6k to $18.3k. Conversations per program rise from 28.6 to 100 (~136 -> ~475 founder hours). The exiting OCM's routing of EOL demand to ATP, Alliance Memory and EDX (Micron) and to Rochester, Sourceability and Flip (Intelligent Memory) points the same way.
responses.action: p_program 0.35 -> 0.10 (used only in what-ifs, since L1 is off). Micross is recorded as a direct competitor for L1, not a white-label partner. Track C3 is moot. Sources logged in research/sources/p5r-legacy-dram-diebank.jsonl.

responses.response: Reproduced exactly with DD6's own model (model §10h imports models/private-moe-appliance.py). At 65 h/month DD6 goes full-time at m23 with $253.7k m36 ARR. At 55 h it goes full-time at m33 ($145.4k). At 45 h it never goes full-time ($122.8k). [Phase 7 gate note, 2026-11-01: those figures used DD6's Phase 4 inputs. After DD6's own round-2 red team, model §10h gives DD6 full-time never at 65, 55 and 45 h/month, with m36 ARR $63.9k / $56.2k / $45.3k.] DD7's Plan A used ~20-30 founder hours a month, and its ~50-hour kill test (2026-11-02 to 11-30) collides with DD6's and DD2's tests on the same dates. Keeping DD7 as a side line would cost the PRIMARY 10 months, or its full-time switch altogether, in exchange for a wedge that never pays the founder. DD2, the host DD7 was to be attached to, was itself downgraded in round 1.
responses.action: DD7 gets zero founder hours. The 29-day kill test is withdrawn (saving ~$6k and ~50 hours). Any residual L2 rep line may be considered only after DD6's K1 result is in and DD6 has failed, and only after the K0 employer carve-out. §0, §10 and §11 rewritten.

responses.response: Valid. As with RT-HYP-DD7-05 and RT-VET-DD7-05, Track A's pass bar ('a rep or distribution agreement' and 'wafer or KGD terms') does not test authorized-aftermarket status under DFARS 252.246-7008. That status needs the OCM's permission to make or sell the part after EOL using transferred wafers, tooling or test data. The reviewer adds evidence that the moat is unlikely to be granted at all. The OCMs likely to reply are extending lines, not exiting: Winbond is sold out through 2027 with customers asking for LTAs to 2030 (TrendForce, 2026-08-07), and ISSI supports DDR4/LPDDR4 to 2038. They have no EOL to authorize. The exiting OCM, Micron, has placed EOL continuity with established houses: e2v (2013), ATP (2015, 2018), Alliance Memory and EDX Electronics. The EDX item is reviewer-cited; I did not verify it. I put the chance that a new U.S. entity gets authorized-aftermarket rights on a DRAM part within 15 months at <=5% [ESTIMATE].
responses.action: Track A rewritten (reopen condition: a written OCM statement of willingness to grant authorized-aftermarket or authorized-distributor-for-EOL status on a named part). C-91's moat (score 4) is recorded as unsupported for an entrant. 'What must be true' #1 is restated.

responses.response: Valid, and the same finding as RT-HYP-DD7-07. The $6.3-25.4M is die or part value with an unsourced 10% memory share, not the founder's fee pool. Model §10i: winning all ~127 memory life-of-need cases a year would add $1.14M of program ARR plus $0.25-1.01M of agency fees. A 3-5% share is $34-57k of new ARR a year, which is the Phase 4 model's own answer. Program fees do not scale with program size, so L1 + L2 were capped near $1-2M a year even at 100% national share. With L1 killed, the addressable pool for this founder is zero.
responses.action: §3 ceiling restated as a fee pool (model §10i). The 'Rochester-scale ceiling' selection reason for DD7 is recorded as unsupported in §14.

responses.response: Valid. Model §10g: the BULL case returns 7.31x on Phase 4 inputs and 7.22x revised, at 1.5x year-10 revenue. That is ~22.0% (21.9%) a year gross if all capital went in at t0, before dilution, an option pool and a hi-rel co-founder's equity, over a horizon longer than a normal fund life. Revised BASE Plan B is worse than Phase 4: 0.29x on $11.49M of outside capital (was 0.46x on $8.11M), GLUT 0.24x, SEVERE 0.19x, year-10 EBITDA -$1.10M, and EBITDA negative in every year. The 4 design-ins x 1,000 units grid cell falls from 4.04x to 2.73x, so not even the 'venture case' clears 3x. The competitor list was short: 3D Plus is added. Micron Manassas (U.S. 1-alpha DDR4/LP4 for defense, qualified output expected end-2026) and ISSI (to 2038) give a 2028 NewSpace designer a supported part, which erodes the locked-die premise for new designs.
responses.action: The open door to the MCM is narrowed. Reopen C-65 only if a hi-rel co-founder brings an existing x72 design-in, and >=3 NewSpace or rugged buyers issue evaluation LOIs at >=$1,200 for an unflown part. 3D Plus added to §5 (via §14). BULL and grid recomputed on revised inputs (model §6, §10g).

responses.response: Valid. Plan C needs a full-time founder (the day job ends), a personal guarantee on a ~$3.6M SBA loan from someone with under $50k of capital, $410k of outside equity nobody has been asked for, and a target nobody has named. Resurgent, the template, went to Flip in 2023, and Lansdale makes no DRAM. The only asset that matters, the OCM licence, may carry change-of-control clauses (unchecked). Its DSCR is 0.85 in GLUT and 0.45 in SEVERE against a ~1.25 lender bar, and the $5M SBA cap is unverified. No input changes rescue this. It fails on founder constraints, not on arithmetic.

responses.response: Valid. On a DO-254 avionics board or an FDA-validated device, the qualified item is a packaged part number: package construction, substrate, mold compound, wire, MSL rating, marking and the OCM's final test. A banked die re-packaged in a new FBGA at a U.S. OSAT is a different part. Its construction change triggers the delta qualification or change-impact review the buyer wanted to avoid, unless the maker holds OCM-transferred package designs and test programs, which come only with authorization (§6). Unauthorized die banking can therefore serve only hybrids and MCMs. Those makers run their own banks: Teledyne under its Micron life-extension program since 2013, Mercury, Frontgrade, and Micross with ~15M die at Apopka. Track B's question would have scored demand that a re-packaged die cannot serve.
responses.action: The §1 'locked die' claim is corrected (via §14): for DO-254/FDA the lock is on the packaged part, so an unauthorized die bank cannot serve it. Track B rewritten as the reviewer proposes ('Would you accept a part built by a third party from banked die in a new package, without re-qualifying the board, and what delta qualification would you require?'). It needs >=3 of 10 written yes answers with no more than a paper delta, and it is now a reopen condition.

responses.response: Valid, and model §10d reproduces the reviewer's re-runs on Phase 4 inputs exactly. All-in pull cost of $15/die gives unit GM 30.8%, IRR -0.5% and 0.98x. $21.50 gives 14.5% and -7.2%. $30 gives -6.8% and -19.9%. On Phase 4 inputs the IRR break-even is $14.48/die all-in (unit GM is zero at $27.30), so C1's $15 pass line would have passed a bank that the model itself says loses money. The stack also omitted wafer-sort-program re-probe with a product probe card, window-BGA (board-on-chip) assembly for center-pad die, hot and cold at-speed insertions, burn-in and JESD47 qualification. I carry (c)+(d) at $10/die, the low end of the reviewer's $10-20. With all Phase 5 revisions together (pull $21.50, yield 0.90, 2.0x multiple, $5k/yr surveillance, whole-wafer opening), the bank bought at m20 in BASE has unit GM -12.8%, IRR -26.6% and a 0.10x cash multiple. GLUT is -109% GM and -99.4% IRR. The IRR break-even pull cost on revised inputs is $1.53/die, below even the Rochester-scale $2. No bank is bought in any scenario. A title-taking bank at U.S. low-volume pull costs is not viable for an entrant.
responses.action: Named leg L3 (title-taking bank) killed. burnin_hotcold_unit 0 -> $10/die. Track C1 is withdrawn, and the reopen condition is an all-in quote at or below the revised break-even. Plan B carries no bank in any scenario (model §5 and §10d). New pull_breakeven() helper.

responses.response: Valid. A 91% module yield assumed each of nine die is 99% good after a -55 to 125 C screen. Distributor KGD is wafer-probed at commercial or industrial temperature, without burn-in or a 125 C screen, so the hot screen happens after sealing, on a 9-die part that cannot be reworked. Model §10e reproduces the reviewer's re-runs on Phase 4 inputs. Module yield 0.76 gives unit cost $586/$515/$412 and GM 34.8/42.8/54.3% (the reviewer's 54.2% is rounding). Yield 0.63 gives 21.4/31.0/44.8%. KGD at parity at 0.76 yield gives 30.8% at m1. The heritage point also holds. Teledyne's die-revision control comes from a Micron life-extension agreement. Distributor KGD has no revision lock, so TID, SEL and hot-retention data recur per die revision and wafer lot, a cost the one-time NRE did not carry. Combining this with RT-PHY-DD7-01 and -02, revised MCM GM is 18.7/26.7/38.2% (m1/m36/m60).
responses.action: mcm_yield 0.91 -> 0.76 (0.97^9); new mcm_lot_requal_yr $75k/yr from the evaluation lot onward [ESTIMATE: one TID + SEL + hot-retention campaign a year]. The L4 reopen condition adds a KGD supply agreement with die-revision change notification and wafer-lot traceability, plus <=1% per-die fallout at a 125 C screen.

A rep or distribution offer is scored only as L2 (§10, §11).

responses.response: Correct. A 9-die x72 module sold into QML programs is a hybrid (multichip) microcircuit under MIL-PRF-38534 (Class H/K), not MIL-PRF-38535, which covers monolithic parts. The alternative is a plastic part screened to NASA EEE-INST-002, as Teledyne's is. 38534 certification attaches to a DLA-audited assembly line, so a fabless entrant must build at a house that holds it. Per the reviewer, the U.S. holders largely overlap with the §5 competitors. I did not check DLA's QML-38534 listing, so that is [UNVERIFIED]. The $1.4M NRE and $80 assembly carried no line-access, audit or competitor-margin item. With RT-PHY-DD7-01's stacked build, assembly plus screening is now $310/unit, above the reviewer's $290 bar.
responses.action: §7 corrected to MIL-PRF-38534 / EEE-INST-002 (via §14). mcm_nre_total $1.4M -> $1.6M for QML-38534 line access [ESTIMATE]. The L4 reopen condition adds a quote from an independent 38534 or EEE-INST-002-capable house that does not sell x72 DDR4, with NRE <=$2M and assembly plus screening <=$290.
